source: Camerer et al. (2018) Social Sciences Replication Project, via FLoRA atlas record of Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory
finding: The one replication on record of the Sparrow 2011 'Google Stroop' result failed. The point estimate had the same sign as the original but was not significant.
numbers: First data round p=0.2647; rounds 1 and 2 pooled p=0.4493. Replicated experiment was Study 1 only (difficult questions slow colour naming of computer words).
limits: Did not test the content-vs-location memory experiments. Original authors and Camerer et al. note design differences (cognitive load manipulation) cannot be ruled out. Hesselmann (2020, PeerJ) reports a second non-replication; I could not open that page (403).
agent_relevance: Do not build on the claim that having a tool primes tool-related thinking. The solid part of the offloading story is behavioural (what people choose to store), not this priming effect.

source: Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory
finding: People told that typed facts would be saved remembered the facts less and remembered where they were saved better.
numbers: Original Science report of four studies (cited from memory of the paper, not opened this session).
limits: Only the Study 1 Stroop result has a formal replication attempt (failed, b01). I found no large preregistered replication of the recall-vs-expected-access result.
agent_relevance: Treat 'storage expectation reduces memory of content, raises memory of location' as plausible but unconfirmed. Design hint only: keep an index of where things are.

source: Ngai & Gilbert (2026) Metacognitive training facilitates optimal cognitive offloading
finding: A five-trial intervention (predict your memory, then get feedback) reduced over-use of reminders in Experiment 1 and replicated in Experiment 2. Making predictions without feedback did not help.
numbers: Exp 1 N=164 (82 per group, 189 tested): reminder bias lower with feedback, t(162)=2.22, p=.01 one-tailed, d=.347; absolute bias d=0.26, p=.048. Exp 2 N=416, four groups: feedback pattern replicated; predictions alone ineffective. Feedback group's metacognitive-bias benefit gone at post-task (d=.022).
limits: Online task with points, one-tailed preregistered tests. The metacognitive-bias effect did not last to the end of Exp 1. Effects are small to medium.
agent_relevance: Offloading choice is biased and trainable. Our agent should decide to write a note or call a tool from a calibrated estimate of its own error rate, with feedback from past outcomes, not from raw confidence.

source: Ngai & Gilbert (2026), literature summary of the optimal-offloading paradigm (Gilbert et al. 2020; Ball 2022; Kirk 2021; Sachdeva & Gilbert 2020, 2024)
finding: Across studies using the optimal-offloading task, people over-use external reminders: they pick the reminder even when internal memory would pay more. The bias is stable within person over time. Low confidence in memory drives reminder use even when confidence is unrelated to real accuracy.
numbers: Six or more studies cited as consistent. In Exp 1, no-feedback group correlation between metacognitive bias and reminder bias r(80)=-.275, p=.006 (one-tailed).
quote: participants are biased towards excessive use of reminders
limits: Study list and effect sizes are the authors' summary; I did not open each primary paper. Paradigm is one memory task with a small reward trade-off.
agent_relevance: Agents show the mirror risk: they may over-trust tools or under-trust their context. Offloading should be a priced choice (cost of a tool call vs error rate), checked against measured accuracy.

source: Zhu, Li, Dong, Chang & Fan (2026) Dependent vs autonomous cognitive offloading to generative AI
finding: Handing core thinking to AI (dependent offloading) tracked lower intrinsic motivation and poorer perceived outcomes. Using AI as a scaffold while keeping the thinking (autonomous offloading) tracked better perceived outcomes. Both gave similar immediate benefit, so the harm is hard to see in the moment.
numbers: Three-wave time-lagged survey, N=589 students and early-career workers. Metacognitive monitoring weakened the link to agency transfer but did not buffer the motivation link.
limits: Self-reported outcomes, correlational, no performance test. Not a test of memory or accuracy.
agent_relevance: Human-side warning about delegating the whole task. For our agent the analogue is a role split where the model keeps the reasoning slot and the program holds state and checks.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: Essay writing with an LLM, a search engine or no tool gave different EEG connectivity. Connectivity scaled down with external support. LLM users were worse at quoting their own essays.
numbers: 54 participants in 3 groups (18 each) over sessions 1-3; 18 completed session 4 (LLM-to-Brain and Brain-to-LLM swap). Full essay ownership: 16/18 brain-only, 6/18 search, 9/18 LLM; no ownership 3/18 LLM.
limits: Small N, preprint under review, EEG inference about engagement is indirect, only 18 in the crossover. Not a learning-outcome test.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence on the cost side of offloading. Do not use as a design rule.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: In Tetris, players rotate pieces on screen more than needed to place them. The extra rotations are epistemic actions: they reveal the shape faster than mental rotation or waiting.
numbers: Early rotation uncovers a piece's full image 150 to 300 ms earlier than waiting. Each piece type is rotated more than half its possible rotations, above the expected number. Rotation often starts within 400-600 ms of the piece appearing, before planning could be finished.
limits: Few expert players, one real-time game; I found no controlled replication. The mental-rotation speed comparison is argued from timing, not measured on the same players.
agent_relevance: Acting on the world to see more can be cheaper than thinking harder. For the agent: run a probe (execute code, test an input) as an action that reveals information, rather than reasoning about what it would show.

source: Fansher, Shah & Helie (preprint) Effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: External (computer) presentation of Tower of Hanoi helped completion but not move quality, and shifted strategy. Solving mentally was slower between moves but pushed toward goal-recursion strategy on the next problem.
numbers: Experiment 1: 123 valid observations in four groups (CC 35, CM 28, MM 30, MC 30). 4-disk progress computer M=4.00 vs mental 3.61, t(35)=2.44, p=.02. Move-count difference not significant, t(116.39)=1.14, p=.26. Time between moves 14.04 s mental vs 7.58 s computer, t(75.99)=-5.62, p<.001.
limits: Online sample; the spoken-move protocol confounds timing. Preprint, year approximate; final published form not checked.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: an external representation raises speed and completion but can reduce strategy learning. Reasoning that will be reused should be generated, not only displayed.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: The unit of analysis for remembering approach speeds is the whole cockpit: speed card, booklet, gross-weight display, bugs and two pilots. Memory is spread over these and their coordination.
numbers: Descriptive case study of an MD-80 descent; no sample statistics.
limits: Observational case study with no control condition. The claim is a framing, not a measured effect.
agent_relevance: Design view: put memory in checkable artefacts with a defined hand-off. This is the argument for the program holding state, not the model.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) collective intelligence factor and its critics: Credé & Howardson (2017); Barlow & Dennis (2016); Bates & Gupta (2017); Rowe et al. (2021); Graf et al. (2019), as summarised in a 2025 paper
finding: Original claim: a single c factor explains group performance, driven by social sensitivity and equal turn-taking rather than member IQ. Independent work found weaker support: less variance explained, low task reliability, failure to replicate in virtual groups, and multi-factor structures.
numbers: Original: 192 groups of 3-5, c explains about 43-44% of variance; criterion tasks r=0.52 (checkers), r=0.28 (architecture). Average member intelligence vs c: r=0.15 in original; Rowe 2021 meta-analysis r from -0.05 to 0.34. Graf 2019 meta-analysis: 3 factors, not 1. LePine 2008: 138 studies, 3 team-process factors.
limits: Second-hand figures read from the introduction of the 2025 paper, not from each primary source.
agent_relevance: The 'social skills beat smart members' story is contested. Do not assume voter diversity or conversational balance helps a group of agents.

source: Zhu-line dyad study (2025) A recipe for dyadic collective intelligence for well-structured tasks
finding: In 105 minimal-group dyads on well-structured tasks, member intelligence and confidence were the strongest predictors of dyad performance. Social sensitivity partly replicated. Equal turn-taking and proportion of women did not.
numbers: N=210 participants in 105 dyads (89% strangers), mean age 20.8. Block 1: social sensitivity beta=0.39, p<.001; all-female dyads beta=-0.85, p<.01; R2=0.23. Final models R2 up to 0.60-0.63; confidence beta 0.63 in one model. Better-than-individual dyads let the more competent member dominate.
limits: Undergraduate sample, two-person groups, well-structured tasks only. Authors say results depend on task type. First author name not verified.
agent_relevance: On well-structured problems the group helps when the more competent member's answer wins. Supports check-based selection over equal-weight votes (G4/G5).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Annotated 1600+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks and built a 14-mode failure taxonomy in 3 groups: system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification.
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source systems. Inter-annotator kappa=0.88 on 150 traces; LLM judge kappa=0.77. Modes: step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, not recognizing completion 12.4%, ignoring task requirements 11.8%.
limits: Benchmarks mostly coding and math; frameworks as of 2024-25; LLM-judge annotation at scale.
agent_relevance: Direct match to the distributed-cognition problem: communication between agents is where it breaks. A single agent with an external program avoids the inter-agent failure group.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) intervention case studies, Appendix H
finding: Fixing roles and adding a verification step helped but only modestly. The authors say these are not substantial improvements.
numbers: ChatDev ProgramDev-v0 (32 tasks): baseline 25.0%, improved prompts 34.4%, new cyclic topology 40.6%. HumanEval: 89.6, 90.3, 91.5. AG2 GSM-Plus GPT-4: 84.75 baseline, 89.75 prompt, 85.50 topology; GPT-4o: 84.25, 89.00, 88.83.
limits: Small task set; table was read from merged layout text so the row pairing is my best reading. Main text also quotes +9.4% and +15.6%.
agent_relevance: Cheap structural fixes (explicit verifier, loop until a checker passes) give most of the gain. Matches our rule that a program ends the loop.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Across 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures and 3 LLM families, whether more agents help depends on the task. Coordination helps decomposable tasks and hurts sequential ones. Centralized checking contains error spread.
numbers: Relative change vs single agent: +80.8% (financial reasoning, centralized) to -70.0% (sequential planning, independent). All multi-agent variants degrade planning by -39% to -70%. Independent agents amplify errors 17.2x vs 4.4x centralized. Above 45% single-agent accuracy extra agents give negative returns (beta=-0.236, p=0.004). Web navigation decentralized +9.2%. Cross-validated R2=0.373; best architecture predicted for 87% of held-out configs.
limits: R2 is modest; fixed budget per cell; the 45% threshold is an empirical fit, not a law.
agent_relevance: Best single quantitative guide: default to one agent, add more only for parallel decomposable work, keep one verifier gate. Agrees with the schema.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five multi-agent debate methods were compared with chain-of-thought and self-consistency over 9 benchmarks and 4 models. Debate usually lost, even with more compute. Mixing different models helped.
numbers: 36 settings (4 models x 9 benchmarks): no MAD method beats CoT in more than 20% of settings; SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15%. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: AgentVerse +0.85%, all other frameworks at least -3.60% vs CoT. Self-consistency usually top.
limits: Prompt formats follow each method's original setup; size of the heterogeneity gain not extracted.
agent_relevance: Re-test of the debate claim at matched compute (b17): it mostly fails. Prefer independent samples plus code voting; if diversity is wanted, vary the model, not the persona.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Benchmark of debate strategies against single agent, self-consistency and Medprompt on MedQA and other sets. The authors conclude debate does not reliably beat simpler prompting and is sensitive to hyperparameters.
numbers: Abstract-level finding; MedQA accuracy plotted against API calls. I did not extract per-method figures.
limits: Only the abstract claim was read closely.
agent_relevance: Second independent source for b15.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: The founding positive result: three agents and two debate rounds beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, grade-school math and chess.
numbers: Arithmetic % / GSM8K % / chess score: single 67.0 / 77.0 / 91.4; reflection 72.1 / 75.0 / 102.1; majority 69.0 / 81.0 / 102.2; debate 81.8 / 85.0 / 122.9. GSM8K debate vs single +8 points; standard errors about 3.5-4.2.
limits: Weak baselines. Later work (b15, b16) finds the advantage mostly disappears against CoT and self-consistency at matched compute.
agent_relevance: Shows the first big claim and why it needs a matched-compute re-test before we adopt it.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction looked good only when the correct label decided when to stop. Without it, the model's own review lowered accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: standard 75.9, round 1 75.1, round 2 74.7. CommonSenseQA: 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5.
limits: Tables read from merged layout text; check oracle-row pairing before quoting. Two rounds only.
agent_relevance: A second head that is the same model is not an independent check. Revise only from real external output (G2, G4).

source: Li et al. (2024) More Agents Is All You Need (Agent Forest)
finding: Plain sampling and voting scales with the number of agents. Gains grow with task difficulty.
numbers: Accuracy gains from more agents: GSM8K +12 to +24 points, MATH +6 to +10, MMLU +5 to +11, Chess +1 to +4, HumanEval +4 to +9. Llama2-13B reaches 59% on GSM8K by ensemble.
limits: Gains shrink as base accuracy rises; same-model samples share errors (our G4).
agent_relevance: Cheap, code-selected aggregation is the version of many heads that holds up. Use it only where answers can be compared exactly.

source: Li, Lin, Xia & Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents (Self-MoA)
finding: Aggregating several samples from the single best model beat mixing different models. Mixing lowers average quality.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6% over MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0; average +3.8% across MMLU, CRUX, MATH.
limits: Contrasts with b15, where model heterogeneity helped debate. The difference likely lies in the quality gap between models.
agent_relevance: Rival result: diversity is valuable only if the added voices are as good.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
finding: With no direct communication, LLM groups showed emergent higher-order structure only when given personas plus an instruction to think about what others might do. Success needs both synergy and redundancy.
numbers: Group guessing game; main runs N=10 agents, T=1, GPT-4.1 (also Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3 tested). Each extra group member lowers odds of success by about 8% (OR=0.92, p<1e-16); each temperature unit raises odds 50% (OR=1.50). Synergy x redundancy interaction beta=0.24, p=0.014.
limits: One toy task; the author warns against human-like cognition claims; results depend on the prompt.
agent_relevance: Group size hurts, as in human groups. Theory-of-mind prompting was the only moderator that built useful structure. Weak support for any multi-persona design.

source: Shang et al. (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? CoThinker (cognitive load theory)
finding: A multi-agent design that splits load and uses a shared working memory helped on high-load reasoning tasks, while coordination overhead dominated on low-load instruction tasks.
numbers: Gemini-1.5-Pro Math: IO 60.9, CoT 62.4, MAD 69.4, DMAD 70.0, CoThinker 75.3. Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B Math: IO 33.8, MAD 38.6, CoThinker 37.7.
limits: Authors' own method; table columns were merged in extraction, so I quote only rows I could pair with confidence.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: coordination pays only when task load is high. Supports a gate that engages a second agent on a difficulty signal, not by default.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM)
finding: Agents that retrieve other agents' stored trajectories succeed more and use fewer steps, with no joint training.
numbers: ALFWorld success 47% to 55% (+8.0 points), steps 11.77 to 11.18 with single-stage retrieval; reranked variant up to +17.2 points over no retrieval, steps 10.35. WebArena single-stage 20.5%, reranker equal with 19.91 steps.
limits: Settings and models vary; gain depends on a capability gap between producer and consumer. Two-column PDF text was messy.
agent_relevance: The most direct LLM version of transactive memory. A shared searchable trajectory store is the part of distributed cognition with a measured benefit.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Program statement: cognition is distributed across people, artefacts and time; study the whole system.
numbers: No new experiments (not read in depth).
limits: Framework, not a test.
agent_relevance: Background for the design view only.

source: Risko & Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading, Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Review of when people offload and what it costs and gains. Page could not be opened (403).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Left as a pointer so the next pass can read it.
agent_relevance: Standard citation for offloading costs and benefits.
